title: The Greenhouse Bug Detectives
markdown:
The Sunny Meadow Science Club greenhouse was Zara’s favourite place. It smelled of warm earth and the sweet perfume of sun-ripened blossoms. Sunlight came through the glass roof in golden ribbons, and the broad velvety leaves of her prize-winning moonpetals usually hummed with a soft silvery sheen, as if they were pleased with themselves and saw no reason to hide it. Beside her, Cora the jackdaw hopped from one worn gardening boot to another, sleek black feathers gleaming like polished obsidian. Cora was an excellent observer. She noticed the smallest, most important things, including drips, beetles, and robots who were having an off morning.

Today the greenhouse sighed.

The moonpetals drooped, leaves curling as if to hide. Nearby, Grover the gardening robot whirred a sound that was almost a groan. His watering can hung limp.

“Oh, Grover,” Zara whispered. “You’ve watered the sun-chime flowers again. They don’t need a soaking. The moonpetals are thirsty.” She touched a leaf. Dry as old paper.

Teacher Lin knelt, brow gentle. “Grover is usually so precise. He follows his programming. Something has gone wrong.”

Zara hated unhappy plants. Grover was meant to water what looked dry. The moonpetals looked like parchment. He had given them a mean little sprinkle and drowned the sun-chimes, who liked a drink but not a flood.

Cora cocked her head at Grover’s control panel, a small screen of coloured lights.

“Caw. Look. This bit. Wiggly. Not straight like the others.”

An emerald line flickered in an irregular stutter. Teacher Lin followed the beak.

“That,” she said softly, “is a bug. Not a beetle. A tiny knot in Grover’s instructions. A mistake that sends him to the wrong plants.”

Zara’s voice wobbled. “How do we fix it?”

“We become bug detectives. We trace his steps, one by one, and find where the wiggly light leads him astray.”

Bug detectives sounded braver than worry. Cora nudged Zara’s hand. “Caw. I see things.”

They followed the glowing recipe on Grover’s panel, light by light, the way you follow a cake if you do not want to ice it before it is baked. If this is true, then do that. If the soil is dry, water. A bug, Teacher Lin said, might confuse him about which soil counted as dry, or which plant came next on the list.

Cora’s keen eyes spotted it first: a line meant for watering the sun-chimes sitting just before the moonpetal steps, so Grover soaked the wet flowers first and arrived at the thirsty ones with an empty can, or nearly, which is no use to a moonpetal at all.

“There!” Zara’s voice came clear. Not mysterious. Order, in the wrong order. Fixable.

Teacher Lin showed Zara how to adjust Grover’s settings, the buttons small and serious under greenhouse light. Zara’s hands trembled, then thought of silvery leaves longing for moisture, and steadied. She was fixing it. She was helping her plants. A soft whirr. Grover sprang to life again, movements purposeful. He went directly to the moonpetals and gave them a perfect generous shower of cool water. Droplets kissed the leaves; they perked, reaching. Then he moved to the sun-chimes and gave them a much gentler sprinkle, just what they needed, which is a kind of apology a robot can make without saying sorry.

“He’s doing it!”

Cora fluttered a miniature parade around Zara’s head.

Teacher Lin beamed. “You found the bug and fixed it. Debugging. Finding the mistake in the instructions and putting the steps back where they belong.”

Zara watched the moonpetals glisten. The nervousness had gone the way of Grover’s empty-can confusion: corrected. She did not announce a career in secrets. She watched Grover check the soil like a robot who had remembered his manners, and Cora peck a stray drip off a boot, and the greenhouse, which had been sighing, took up its old quiet hum, the contented kind that needs water in the right order and nowhere else.
characters: Zara (trail naturalist), Cora (jackdaw), Teacher Lin (teacher), Grover (gardening robot)
